meaning: Marks the topic of the sentence
explanation: は sets up what the rest of the sentence will be about; it doesn't necessarily mark the grammatical subject. Contrast with が, which introduces new information or highlights the subject itself. New learners often overuse は where が is needed, especially with question words (誰が来ますか, not 誰は).
example_reading: わたしはがくせいです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Pronounced "wa", not "ha", when used as this particle.

meaning: Marks the subject, especially new information; also used with 好き/欲しい/わかる/できる
explanation: が answers "who/what" questions and introduces new, previously unmentioned information, where は would sound off if the topic is already established. It's also required (not optional) with a fixed set of predicates: 好き, 嫌い, 欲しい, わかる, できる, あります/います — even though these look like objects in English, Japanese treats them as the grammatical subject.
example_reading: ねこがいます。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Contrasts with は by highlighting the subject itself.

meaning: Marks the direct object of a transitive verb
explanation: を marks what receives the action of a transitive verb. A small set of motion verbs (歩く、走る、渡る、散歩する) also take を to mark the space passed through rather than a destination, e.g. 公園を歩きます (I walk through the park) — a common point of confusion with に/で.
example_reading: ぱんをたべます。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Pronounced "o", not "wo", in modern speech.

meaning: Marks a specific point in time
explanation: に attaches to specific, countable points in time (clock times, dates, weekdays) but is dropped with relative time words like 今日、明日、今、毎日 — you say 月曜日に行きます but just 明日行きます, without に.
example_reading: しちじにおきます。
example_meaning: I get up at seven o'clock.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Not used with relative time words like 今日/明日.

explanation: に and へ are interchangeable for destinations in casual speech, but に is also required for the "point" side of many other patterns (existence, giving/receiving, indirect objects), so it's worth mastering に first.
example_reading: がっこうにいきます。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Interchangeable with へ for destinations.

explanation: へ emphasizes the general direction of travel rather than the specific endpoint. In everyday speech, に and へ are largely interchangeable for destinations, so don't worry too much about picking the "wrong" one casually.
example_reading: にほんへいきます。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Pronounced "e", not "he", when used as this particle.

meaning: Marks where an action takes place
explanation: で marks where an action happens, while に marks where something exists or is located — compare 部屋で勉強します (I study in the room, action) with 部屋にいます (I am in the room, existence). Mixing these up is one of the most common N5 particle mistakes.
example_reading: としょかんでべんきょうします。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Contrast with に, which marks the location of existence.

meaning: Marks the means, tool, or material used
explanation: で also covers the tool, method, or material used to do something, extending beyond transportation to writing tools (ペンで書く), languages (日本語で話す), and payment methods (カードで払う).
example_reading: ばすでいきます。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Also used for materials: 紙で作ります (I make it out of paper).

meaning: Marks a companion for an action
explanation: と requires an animate companion who actively takes part in the action together with the speaker; for a tool or instrument, use で instead — 友達と話す (talk with a friend) vs 電話で話す (talk by phone).
example_reading: ともだちとはなします。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Requires a person or animate companion, not a tool.

meaning: Connects nouns into a complete, exhaustive list
explanation: と creates a complete, closed list — パンと卵を買いました implies bread and eggs were the only things bought. If other unlisted items might also be present, use や instead.
example: パンと卵を買いました。
example_reading: ぱんとたまごをかいました。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Lists everything; compare や for partial lists.

meaning: "Also, too"; replaces は, が, or を
explanation: も replaces は、が、or を entirely (it never stacks with them) and can appear on multiple parts of a sentence to mean "both... and...": 兄も姉もいます (I have both an older brother and an older sister).
example_reading: わたしもがくせいです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Can be repeated: AもBも (both A and B).

meaning: Marks a starting point in time or space
explanation: から marks a starting point for time, place, or motion, and is very commonly paired with まで to define a range (九時から五時まで). から can separately mean "because" at the end of a full clause — context tells the two uses apart.
example_reading: くじからはじまります。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Often paired with まで.

meaning: Marks an ending point in time or space
explanation: まで marks an endpoint and, unlike から, cannot mean "because." It's almost always learned as a pair with から to express a range.
example_reading: ごじまではたらきます。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Often paired with から.

meaning: Connects two nouns, showing possession or description
explanation: の links any two nouns, not just for possession — it also connects nationality/origin + noun (日本の車), material + noun, and topic + noun, working much like English "of" in reverse order.
example_reading: これはわたしのほんです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Also links nationality/profession + noun: 日本の車。

meaning: Turns a preceding modifier into "the one that..."
explanation: This の stands in for a noun already mentioned so you don't have to repeat it — if someone points at bags and asks どれがいいですか, you can answer 赤いのがいいです instead of repeating かばん.
example_reading: あかいのをください。
example_meaning: Please give me the red one.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Avoids repeating the noun already mentioned.

meaning: Turns a statement into a question
explanation: か simply turns any statement into a question by attaching to the end; word order never changes. か can also connect two nouns to mean "or" (コーヒーか紅茶, coffee or tea).
example_reading: がくせいですか。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: The question mark is usually omitted in writing.

explanation: や lists a few representative items while implying others aren't mentioned — 本やペンがあります suggests notebooks, erasers, etc. might also be there. This softness makes や natural for giving examples rather than a complete inventory.
example: 机の上に本やペンがあります。
example_reading: つくえのうえにほんやぺんがあります。
example_meaning: There are things like books and pens on the desk.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Implies other items are also present.

explanation: だけ is neutral and simply states a limit ("only this many/this much") without extra emotional color, making it the safer default compared to しか, which always forces a negative verb and implies less than expected.
example_reading: ひとつだけください。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Neutral in tone, unlike しか.

explanation: しか must be followed by a negative predicate even though the meaning is positive in English ("only 1000 yen" = 千円しかありません). It often implies the amount is less than hoped for, unlike the neutral だけ.
example_reading: せんえんしかありません。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Always paired with a negative verb.

explanation: ね invites agreement or shared feeling and softens statements, making conversation feel collaborative — but overusing it with someone you don't know well, or in formal writing, can sound overly familiar.
example_reading: いいてんきですね。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Softens statements and invites a response.

explanation: よ asserts something the speaker believes the listener doesn't already know, so it's used to inform, warn, or correct. Using よ with information the listener obviously already knows can sound condescending.
example_reading: あしたはやすみですよ。
example_meaning: Tomorrow is a day off, you know.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Can sound pushy if overused with strangers.

explanation: です is the polite form of the copula だ, used after nouns and な-adjectives. Unlike English "to be," it never conjugates for person or number, only for tense and politeness (です/だ, でした/だった).
example_reading: あれはやまです。
notes: The plain equivalent is だ.

explanation: じゃ is a contraction of では common in speech; ではありません is preferred in writing or formal contexts, while じゃありません and the even more casual じゃない are typical of everyday conversation.
formation: Noun/な-Adj + じゃありません
example_reading: せんせいじゃありません。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: ではありません is more formal/written.

explanation: でした is simply です shifted to the past; the tense sits on the copula itself, not on the noun or な-adjective in front of it, which stays unchanged.
example_reading: きのうはあめでした。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Negative past is 〜じゃありませんでした。

reading: じゃありませんでした
explanation: This combines the negative and the past together; casual speech often shortens it to じゃなかった(です), worth recognizing even if not the focus here.
formation: Noun/な-Adj + じゃありませんでした
example: 休みじゃありませんでした。
example_reading: やすみじゃありませんでした。
example_meaning: It was not a day off.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Longer, but very common in speech.

reading: いけいようし（げんざい）
explanation: い-adjectives conjugate on their own, without needing です for grammatical correctness — 面白い is already a complete sentence; です only adds politeness, unlike with nouns/な-adjectives where だ/です carries real grammatical weight.
example_reading: このほんはおもしろいです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: です here just adds politeness, not tense.

explanation: Drop the final い and add くない; the one irregular case to remember is いい (good), which becomes よくない, not いくない.
formation: い-Adj stem + くない(です)
example: この本は面白くないです。
example_reading: このほんはおもしろくないです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: いい becomes よくない, an irregular change.

explanation: Drop the final い and add かった; いい again becomes よかった, following the same irregular pattern as the negative form.
formation: い-Adj stem + かった(です)
example: 映画は面白かったです。
example_reading: えいがはおもしろかったです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: いい becomes よかった。

reading: いけいようし（かこひてい）
explanation: Combine both rules: drop い, add くなかった. This four-way table (present/negative/past/past-negative) is the backbone for every い-adjective you'll ever learn.
formation: い-Adj stem + くなかった(です)
example: テストは難しくなかったです。
example_reading: てすとはむずかしくなかったです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Combines the negative and past rules.

reading: なけいようし（かつよう）
meaning: Conjugate a な-adjective like a noun
explanation: な-adjectives behave grammatically like nouns — they take だ/です、じゃない、and だった exactly as a noun would, which is why they're sometimes called "adjectival nouns."
formation: な-Adj + だ/です/じゃない/だった
example_reading: ここはしずかです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: No な appears before です, only before a noun.

meaning: Modify a noun with a な-adjective
explanation: The な only appears when directly modifying a following noun (静かな町); in the predicate position (町は静かです) the な disappears entirely — mixing these two forms up is a very common beginner error.
example_reading: しずかなまちです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: The な is dropped in the predicate form.

meaning: Modify a noun with an い-adjective
explanation: Unlike な-adjectives, い-adjectives attach directly to the following noun with no linking particle at all, in exactly the same form used in the predicate.
example: 面白い映画を見ました。
example_reading: おもしろいえいがをみました。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: No linking word is needed between an い-adjective and a noun.

explanation: ます attaches to the pre-masu stem of the verb (食べ-ます、飲み-ます、し-ます) and is the default polite form for people you don't know well or formal contexts; casual speech uses the plain forms instead.
example_reading: まいにちべんきょうします。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Also expresses future or habitual action.

explanation: A simple negative swap of ます; the ません ending itself never changes form regardless of verb type.
example_reading: おさけをのみません。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: The negative counterpart of ます。

explanation: Past tense sits on ます itself (ます→ました), leaving the verb stem untouched — this regularity is one reason polite forms are often taught before plain forms.
example_reading: きのうべんきょうしました。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: The past form of ます。

explanation: Combines negative and past; there's no casual contraction of this in polite speech, unlike the plain forms.
formation: Verb stem + ませんでした
example: 昨日は行きませんでした。
example_reading: きのうはいきませんでした。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: The past negative form of ます。

meaning: Plain/dictionary form, used before certain grammar and in casual speech
explanation: The dictionary form is also the plain/casual present tense used with friends and family, and it's the form found in dictionaries — it's the base for potential, volitional, and many later grammar patterns.
example_reading: まいにちはしる。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Also the form found in dictionaries.

explanation: Formed differently by verb group (godan verbs shift to the a-stem, e.g. 飲む→飲まない; ichidan verbs drop る and add ない). Mastering this early pays off, since dozens of later patterns (なければ、ないで、なくてもいい) build on it.
example_reading: おさけをのまない。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Base for many N4 patterns like 〜なければ。

explanation: た形 follows the exact same sound-change rules as て形 — once you know て形, た形 is essentially free, since you just swap て/で for た/だ.
example_reading: えいがをみた。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Follows the same sound changes as て形。

meaning: Connective form linking clauses or actions
explanation: Sound changes depend on the verb's final syllable (う/つ/る→って、ぬ/ぶ/む→んで、く→いて、ぐ→いで、す→して), plus irregulars for する→して and 来る→来て. Arguably the single most important form in Japanese, since permission, requests, and progressive tense all attach to it.
example: 朝起きて、顔を洗います。
example_reading: あさおきて、かおをあらいます。
example_meaning: I wake up in the morning and wash my face.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Base for many patterns: てください、ています, etc.

explanation: ましょう proposes a joint action and assumes the listener will likely agree, which is why it's often translated "let's," rather than being a genuine question.
example_reading: いっしょにいきましょう。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Suggests an action to be done together.

explanation: Adding か turns the proposal into an offer or question, checking whether the listener actually wants that action — 行きましょう (let's go, assumed agreement) vs 行きましょうか (shall we go? checking first).
example_reading: まどをあけましょうか。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Offers to do something for the listener.

explanation: Phrasing an invitation as a negative question (ませんか instead of ましょう) is considered more polite, since it leaves the listener room to decline without directly rejecting a proposal.
example: 一緒に映画を見ませんか。
example_reading: いっしょにえいがをみませんか。
example_meaning: Won't you watch a movie with me?
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Softer and more polite than ましょう。

explanation: This nominalizes the verb ("the act of doing X") before stating it "is possible" — grammatically more roundabout than the direct potential form (食べられる), which is why native speakers favor the potential form in casual speech.
formation: Verb (dictionary form) + ことができます
example: 漢字を読むことができます。
example_reading: かんじをよむことができます。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: More formal than the potential verb form.

explanation: For an action currently unfolding, ています behaves like English "-ing": 今、電話で話しています (I am talking on the phone right now).
formation: Verb て form + います
example_reading: いま、ほんをよんでいます。
example_meaning: I am reading a book now.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Also used for repeated habitual actions.

meaning: Describes a resulting state after a change
explanation: For a small set of change verbs (結婚する、住む、知る、持つ), ています instead describes the resulting ongoing state, not an action in progress — 結婚しています means "I am married," not "I am getting married."
formation: Verb て form + います
example_reading: けっこんしています。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Common with verbs like 知る、住む、持つ。

explanation: Literally "even if [I] do X, it's fine" — asking permission this way is indirect and polite by nature. A blunt refusal (だめです) is common, but native speakers often soften a "no" with ちょっと... instead.
formation: Verb て form + もいいです(か)
example: ここで写真を撮ってもいいですか。
example_reading: ここでしゃしんをとってもいいですか。
example_meaning: May I take a photo here?
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Answer with はい、いいですよ or いいえ、だめです。

explanation: てください is polite but fairly direct — appropriate for teachers, service staff, or instructions, but with close friends it can feel unnecessarily formal, where a bare て-form request is more natural.
formation: Verb て form + ください
example: ここに名前を書いてください。
example_reading: ここになまえをかいてください。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Softer than a plain command form.

explanation: A strong, formal prohibition often seen on signs and rules; in casual speech, だめ or ちゃだめ softens the same meaning considerably.
formation: Verb て form + はいけません
example: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません。
example_reading: ここでしゃしんをとってはいけません。
example_meaning: You must not take photos here.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Stronger than ないほうがいいです。

explanation: Built on the plain negative (ない形) plus でください — note this base differs from てはいけません, which uses the plain affirmative て形. Mixing up which base each request pattern needs is a common error.
formation: Verb ない form + でください
example: ここに駐車しないでください。
example_reading: ここにちゅうしゃしないでください。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Common on signs and instructions.

explanation: Turning the request into a negative question (くださいませんか instead of ください) adds a layer of humility, similar to how ませんか softens invitations — useful when asking a favor of someone senior to you.
formation: Verb て form + くださいませんか
example: 窓を開けてくださいませんか。
example_reading: まどをあけてくださいませんか。
example_meaning: Could you please open the window?
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: More formal/humble than てください。

meaning: Expresses the speaker's own desire to do something
explanation: たいです directly expresses the speaker's own first-person desire and behaves like an い-adjective (たかったです、たくないです). It sounds overly direct or even rude used about someone else's wishes, where たがっている is used instead.
example_reading: にほんへいきたいです。
example_meaning: I want to go to Japan.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Not usually used to describe others' desires directly; use たがっている。

explanation: が, not を, marks the desired object because ほしい is grammatically an い-adjective ("desirable/wanted"), not a verb. Like たい, it conjugates as an adjective and is typically reserved for the speaker's own wants.
example: 新しい靴がほしいです。
example_reading: あたらしいくつがほしいです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: が, not を, marks the desired object.

explanation: あります covers all inanimate existence, including abstract events like meetings or parties (パーティーがあります), and is also used idiomatically for "having" something (お金があります), since Japanese doesn't distinguish "there is" from "I have."
example: 机の上に本があります。
example_reading: つくえのうえにほんがあります。
example_meaning: There is a book on the desk.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Also used for events: パーティーがあります。

explanation: います is reserved strictly for animate beings (people, animals) — using あります for a person or pet is a common and noticeable beginner mistake.
example_reading: へやにねこがいます。
example_meaning: There is a cat in the room.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Used for people and animals, not objects.

japanese: これ・それ・あれ・どれ
reading: これ・それ・あれ・どれ
explanation: These follow a consistent こ/そ/あ/ど pattern found across all demonstrative words: こ- near the speaker, そ- near the listener, あ- far from both, ど- the question form — a pattern worth memorizing once, since it recurs everywhere.
example: それは私のかばんです。
example_reading: それはわたしのかばんです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: それ = near the listener, あれ = far from both speakers.

japanese: この・その・あの・どの
reading: この・その・あの・どの
explanation: Unlike これ/それ/あれ/どれ, this set can never stand alone — it must always directly precede a noun, functioning purely as an adjective ("this ~," not "this").
formation: この/その/あの/どの + Noun
example_reading: このほんはおもしろいです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Always followed directly by a noun.

japanese: ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ
reading: ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ
explanation: The same near/far logic applies to places as to things; あそこ specifically implies a place visible or known to both speakers, not just any distant place.
example_reading: ここはわたしのがっこうです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Same near/far pattern as これ・それ・あれ。

japanese: こちら・そちら・あちら・どちら
reading: こちら・そちら・あちら・どちら
explanation: These are the polite register of the this/that series, commonly used to introduce people politely (こちらは田中さんです) or to ask a polite either/or question (どちらがいいですか).
example: こちらは田中さんです。
example_reading: こちらはたなかさんです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Also used politely to mean "which one" (choice).

explanation: 何 shifts to なん before だ/です, before some counters (何人、何時), and before n/d/t sounds generally, while なに is used more as a standalone question or before other consonants — worth listening for in native speech.
example_reading: これはなんですか。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Read なん before です/だ and before some counters.

explanation: だれ is neutral in politeness; どなた is the respectful equivalent used when asking about someone senior or a stranger you're addressing formally.
example_reading: あのひとはだれですか。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: どなた is the more polite equivalent.

explanation: いつ can be answered with anything from a specific date to a vague time expression (今度、いつか), making it more flexible than asking for a specific 何時 or 何日.
example_reading: たんじょうびはいつですか。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Answers can be a date, day, or time expression.

explanation: どこ pairs naturally with に/で/へ depending on whether you're asking about existence, action location, or direction — the particle doesn't change, the following verb determines the meaning.
example_reading: といれはどこですか。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Part of the こそあど series.

explanation: どう is casual; いかが is its polite equivalent, commonly heard from service staff (お飲み物はいかがですか, would you like something to drink?).
example_reading: あじはどうですか。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: いかが is the more polite form.

explanation: いくつ literally counts native-counter items (ひとつ、ふたつ...) up to about ten, and by extension is used to casually ask a young child's age instead of the more adult 何歳。
example: りんごはいくつありますか。
example_reading: りんごはいくつありますか。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Also used to politely ask a child's age.

explanation: いくら asks specifically about price or cost and cannot be used for general quantity — for "how many," use いくつ or a specific counter with 何。
example_reading: これはいくらですか。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Only for prices, not general quantity.

explanation: どうして is more common and neutral in speech; なぜ appears more in writing, formal speech, or when the question carries a slightly more serious or analytical tone.
example: どうして遅れましたか。
example_reading: どうしておくれましたか。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: なぜ is slightly more formal/written.

meaning: Basic numbers 1–10 and beyond (native and Sino-Japanese)
explanation: Japanese numbers combine a native system (ひとつ、ふたつ...) with a Sino-Japanese system (いち、に、さん...) borrowed from Chinese — which one you use depends entirely on the counter word that follows.
example: りんごを三つ買いました。
example_reading: りんごをみっつかいました。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Two number systems exist; the counter decides which to use.

meaning: Native Japanese counter for general objects (1–10)
explanation: This native counter is the default "catch-all" for objects when you don't know the specific counter, but it only goes up to とお (ten); beyond that, switch to Sino-Japanese numbers (じゅういち, etc.).
example: りんごが五つあります。
example_reading: りんごがいつつあります。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Only goes up to とお (ten); use Sino-Japanese numbers after that.

explanation: Almost all counters have irregular readings at 1 and 2, and 人 is a classic example: 一人 (ひとり) and 二人 (ふたり) don't follow the regular いちにん/ににん pattern that resumes from three onward.
example_reading: かぞくはよにんです。
example_meaning: There are four people in my family.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: 一人/二人 have irregular readings (ひとり/ふたり)。

explanation: A subtle but important distinction: 時 answers "at what time," while 時間 answers "for how long" — 三時に会います (I'll meet you at 3 o'clock) vs 三時間待ちます (I'll wait for three hours).
example_reading: さんじかんべんきょうしました。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: 時 = point in time, 時間 = length of time.

explanation: Days of the month have irregular native readings for the first ten days and the 14th, 20th, and 24th (ついたち、ふつか、みっか...はつか) that must be memorized individually.
example_reading: ごがつみっかはやすみです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Many day readings (ついたち、ふつか...) are irregular.

explanation: 歳 and 才 are interchangeable in casual writing, though 歳 is more standard; the one irregular reading to remember is 二十歳 (はたち), breaking from the otherwise regular にじゅっさい pattern.
example_reading: はたちになりました。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: 二十歳 has the special reading はたち。

explanation: そして simply sequences two separate sentences and works for almost any connection, though in very casual speech it can sound slightly bookish compared to just pausing or using それで。
example: 宿題をしました。そして、寝ました。
example_reading: しゅくだいをしました。そして、ねました。
example_meaning: I did my homework. And then, I slept.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Connects full sentences, not just words.

explanation: でも starts a new sentence with a contrast to what was just said; its formal written counterpart is しかし, while だけど is the casual spoken equivalent.
example: 忙しいです。でも、楽しいです。
example_reading: いそがしいです。でも、たのしいです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Casual; しかし is more formal.

explanation: When から attaches to a full clause rather than a noun, it means "because," with the reason stated first and the result following — a direct, personal way to give a reason, slightly less formal than ので.
example_reading: つかれたから、やすみます。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: The reason comes first, the result second.

explanation: This が sits at the end of one clause to soften a contrast or transition into the next, functioning like でも but woven into a single sentence — very common in polite speech to soften bad news or disagreement.
example: この店は安いですが、おいしくないです。
example_reading: このみせはやすいですが、おいしくないです。
example_meaning: This shop is cheap, but it's not tasty.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Softer and more common in speech than でも。

explanation: それから emphasizes that the second event happened after the first in time, making it feel more like a narrated sequence of events than the more neutral そして。
example: 朝ご飯を食べました。それから、学校へ行きました。
example_reading: あさごはんをたべました。それから、がっこうへいきました。
example_meaning: I ate breakfast. After that, I went to school.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: Emphasizes sequence more than そして。

explanation: とても intensifies a positive statement, while あまり must be paired with a negative predicate to mean "not very" — using あまり with a positive verb/adjective is a common learner error when translating "very" directly.
formation: とても + Adj / あまり + Adj + ない
example: 今日はあまり暑くないです。
example_reading: きょうはあまりあつくないです。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: あまり must be paired with a negative verb/adjective.

explanation: よく modifies verbs to mean either "often" (frequency) or "well/skillfully" (quality), with context distinguishing the two, while たくさん specifically quantifies "a lot" of something.
example: 野菜をたくさん食べます。
example_reading: やさいをたくさんたべます。
example_meaning: I eat a lot of vegetables.
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: よく can mean both "often" and "well," depending on context.

explanation: もう pairs naturally with a past-tense verb ("already done"), while まだ pairs with a negative verb for "not yet" (まだしていません) — using まだ with a past-affirmative verb doesn't make grammatical sense.
formation: もう/まだ + Verb (past or negative)
example_reading: もうしゅくだいをしました。
source: Compiled from standard JLPT grammar references; cross-check against Genki/Minna no Nihongo/Bunpro recommended
notes: まだ pairs with a negative for "not yet": まだしていません。
